title: Falling objects
prior_knowledge_summary: Use one sign convention throughout a journey.
Choose and rearrange constant-acceleration equations from signed knowns.
Carry values between stages and delay rounding.
new_learning: Near Earth's surface, a freely falling object has constant downward acceleration g when air resistance is negligible.
For calculations in this lesson use g = 9.81 m s^-2.
Falling from rest means u = 0, not a = 0.
In negligible air resistance, free-fall acceleration is independent of mass.
learning_outcomes: Represent vertical free fall with a consistent sign convention.
Calculate fall time, distance and impact speed using constant-acceleration equations.
Explain why mass does not change free-fall acceleration when air resistance is negligible.
knowledge_boundary: Only one-dimensional downward free fall with negligible air resistance is taught. Upward launch, measuring g and projectile motion are excluded.

visual_rules.reason: Six varied teacher-sketch visuals support direction, signs, equation setup, misconception repair and synthesis.

evidence_basis.canonical_audit: Checked canonical questions, mark schemes and the release-path context diagram. Mapped parts directly support fall time, impact velocity and mass independence.

blocks.title: Which lands first?
body: Imagine two compact metal balls, one twice the mass of the other, released together from the same balcony. Predict which lands first when air resistance is negligible.
It feels natural to choose the heavier ball. Yet both gain downward velocity at the same rate. We need a model that separates mass from the acceleration of free fall.

figure.purpose: Make the opening prediction and equal release conditions visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn side-by-side release of two compact balls of different mass at the same height, with no answer labels.
figure.alt_text: Two differently sized compact balls held at the same balcony height before simultaneous release.

blocks.title: Gravity fixes the acceleration direction
body: Near Earth's surface, an object moving only under gravity is in free fall. When air resistance is negligible, its acceleration is constant and vertically downward.
We use g for the magnitude of this acceleration. In calculations here, g = 9.81 m s^-2. The acceleration vector points downward whether the object is just released or already moving downward.

figure.purpose: Separate the downward acceleration vector from the object's mass.
figure.brief: Teacher sketch of three falling positions at equal time gaps with equal downward acceleration arrows and increasing spacing.
figure.alt_text: A falling ball shown at three times with equal downward acceleration arrows and increasing distances between positions.

blocks.title: Choose down or up as positive
body: The equations do not choose signs for us. If downward is positive, a = +9.81 m s^-2 and a downward displacement is positive. If upward is positive, the same acceleration is a = -9.81 m s^-2 and a downward displacement is negative.
Both choices work. Mixing them does not. Write the positive direction before listing u, v, a, s and t.

figure.purpose: Compare two valid sign conventions for the same fall.
figure.brief: Two-column hand sketch of the same falling ball, one with down positive and one with up positive, showing matching signed a and s.
figure.alt_text: The same downward fall represented with downward-positive and upward-positive sign conventions.

blocks.title: Falling from rest
body: Released from rest means the initial velocity is zero. It does not mean the acceleration is zero. Gravity begins changing the velocity immediately after release.
Formula to remember: v = u + at. Here v and u are velocities in m s^-1, a is acceleration in m s^-2 and t is time in s.
Formula to remember: s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2. Here s is displacement in m.
Formula to remember: v^2 = u^2 + 2as. This is useful when time is not given.

figure.purpose: Show the signed-knowns routine before equation choice.
figure.brief: Annotated u-v-a-s-t table for a released object using downward as positive, with u = 0 highlighted as an initial condition.
figure.alt_text: A signed quantities table for a ball released from rest with downward chosen positive.

blocks.title: A stone dropped down a shaft
body: A stone is released from rest and falls 12.0 m. Take downward as positive. Then u = 0, a = +9.81 m s^-2 and s = +12.0 m.
To find time, use s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2: 12.0 = 0 + 0.5(9.81)t^2, so t = 1.56 s.
To find impact velocity without using the rounded time, use v^2 = u^2 + 2as: v^2 = 2(9.81)(12.0), so v = +15.3 m s^-1. The positive sign means downward in our convention.

figure.purpose: Model a complete calculation layout with signs, units and interpretation.
figure.brief: Handwritten-style worked layout beside a shaft sketch, linking knowns to equation choice and final direction.
figure.alt_text: A stone falling down a 12 metre shaft beside an annotated calculation for time and impact velocity.

blocks.title: Why heavier does not mean faster
body: The heavier-falls-faster idea feels reasonable because heavy objects often beat paper or leaves in air. That comparison changes shape and air resistance as well as mass.

When air resistance is negligible, both compact objects have the same g. With the same u and s, the equations give the same fall time and impact speed. Mass does not appear in these kinematics relationships.

figure.purpose: Contrast a fair free-fall comparison with an air-resistance comparison.
figure.brief: Comparison panel: two compact balls in negligible air resistance versus a ball and flat paper in air, with variables that changed noted simply.
figure.alt_text: A fair comparison of two compact balls and an unfair comparison involving flat paper and air resistance.

blocks.title: Thrown down before free fall
body: A ball is thrown vertically downward at 4.0 m s^-1 from a platform. It falls for 1.5 s. Take downward as positive and g = 9.81 m s^-2.
This is not falling from rest, so u = +4.0 m s^-1, not zero.
Check with average velocity: ((4.0 + 18.7)/2)(1.5) = 17.0 m. The two routes agree.

figure.purpose: Make the reasoning in thrown down before free fall visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for thrown down before free fall.

blocks.title: The free-fall routine
body: First state the positive direction. Next list signed u, v, a, s and t. For a release from rest, set u = 0. Use a = g with the sign set by your convention.

Choose the registered equation that contains the target and knowns. Keep signs and units through the calculation, then state the physical direction. The opening pair of compact balls lands together because both share the same g when air resistance is negligible.

concepts_taught: Free fall near Earth's surface has constant downward acceleration g when air resistance is negligible.
A vertical sign convention determines the signs of acceleration, displacement and velocity.
Free-fall acceleration is independent of mass when air resistance is negligible.
misconceptions_addressed: Released from rest means zero acceleration.
Acceleration becomes larger as an object falls.
A heavier object has a larger free-fall acceleration.
Downward quantities must always be negative.
skills_students_can_now_use: Calculate fall time, distance and impact velocity.
Explain mass independence when air resistance is negligible.
next_lesson_can_assume: Students know g = 9.81 m s^-2 is downward near Earth's surface.
Students can solve downward free-fall calculations from rest with either consistent sign convention.
Students know velocity and acceleration are different quantities.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Students can analyse upward launch or maximum height.
Students can split ascent and descent stages.
Students can describe an experiment to measure g.
